articles.title: Standalone commercial artificial intelligence software for pulmonary nodule detection on chest radiographs: a systematic review.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Pulmonary nodules may be missed on chest radiographs despite their clinical relevance for early lung cancer detection. Commercial artificial intelligence (AI) systems are increasingly available for chest radiograph interpretation, but evidence for their standalone performance remains fragmented across products, datasets, operating thresholds, and comparator designs. PURPOSE: To systematically evaluate the standalone diagnostic performance of commercially available AI software for pulmonary nodule detection on chest radiographs compared with radiologists reading alone, and to identify methodological factors shaping interpretation of the evidence. METHODS: A systematic review was conducted according to PRISMA 2020 guidelines and registered with PROSPERO (CRD420261383905). PubMed, PubMed Central, Scopus, and Web of Science were searched. Eligible studies evaluated commercially available AI systems as standalone detectors for pulmonary nodules on chest radiographs and directly compared their performance with radiologists reading alone using an accepted clinical reference standard. Risk of bias was assessed using an adapted QUADAS-2 framework. Findings were synthesized narratively because of heterogeneity in study design, populations, reference standards, operating thresholds, and outcome measures. RESULTS: Six studies met the inclusion criteria, comprising 12 product-level evaluations across 10 commercial AI systems. Standalone AI performance varied: some evaluations showed AI exceeding radiologist-level performance, others showed no significant difference, and one showed AI below individual reader performance with approximately twice the false-positive rate. In the only standardized within-study comparison of multiple commercial products on the same dataset, four of seven systems significantly exceeded mean radiologist AUC. Standalone AI AUC ranged from 0.79 to 0.93 against a mean reader AUC of 0.81 (95% CI 0.77-0.85), indicating that performance varied among cleared products even when tested under identical conditions. Interpretation was limited by differences in operating thresholds, comparator design, reference standards, study populations, and outcome reporting. Risk-of-bias concerns were common, particularly in patient selection. CONCLUSIONS: In the available peer-reviewed evidence, standalone commercial AI systems for chest radiograph pulmonary nodule detection show variable performance. Evidence remains insufficient to support class-wide standalone deployment because all studies were retrospective or reader-study based, thresholds were inconsistently reported, and real-world false-positive burden remains uncertain. Prospective real world evaluation with clearly reported operating thresholds, standardized comparator designs and complete diagnostic performance are needed.

Integration of Artificial Intelligence in Radiology: A Promising Yet Unprepared Landscape in a Low- and Middle-Income Country.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the perceptions and preparedness of radiology professionals in Pakistan regarding artificial intelligence (AI) integration in radiology, while exploring leadership perspectives on its future role and implementation challenges. METHODS: An explanatory sequential mixed-methods study was conducted using consecutive sampling. In phase one, a webinar was held for radiology professionals across Pakistan, followed by pre- and post-webinar surveys assessing participants' knowledge, perceptions, attitudes, and readiness regarding AI integration in radiology. In phase two, a focused group discussion (FGD) with senior radiology leaders was conducted to further explore survey findings. Quantitative data were analyzed using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test, with p value<0.05 considered statistically significant, while qualitative data underwent thematic framework analysis. Triangulation was performed to integrate and validate findings from both phases. RESULTS: 132 participants completed both surveys, with nearly half being early-career radiologists. Following the webinar, perceptions toward AI shifted significantly. Disagreement with the statement that AI would replace radiologists increased from 43.9% pre-webinar to 87.9% post-webinar. Support for formal AI training also increased substantially. Self-reported knowledge improved, with participants identifying as "very knowledgeable" increasing from 4.5% to 25% after the session (p=0.003). FGD findings highlighted concerns regarding governance, infrastructure, local validation of AI tools, and limited technical expertise. CONCLUSION: Radiology professionals in Pakistan, particularly early-career practitioners, show growing enthusiasm toward AI integration when supported by structured education and training. Leadership perspectives further emphasize the need for locally validated AI solutions, stronger governance frameworks, and integration of AI into radiology curricula for sustainable implementation in low- and middle-income countries.

articles.title: Pre-training everywhere: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning for medical image analysis via target parameter pre-training.
articles.abstract: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) provides an effective approach for adapting pre-trained models to medical imaging tasks while reducing the number of trainable parameters. Additive PEFT methods freeze the pre-trained backbone and introduce a small set of trainable parameters for downstream adaptation. Although few in number, these parameters form the trainable feature-adaptation pathway and are commonly introduced only when supervised fine-tuning begins. We therefore investigate whether they can benefit from task-relevant preparation before supervised adaptation. To this end, we propose Target Parameter Pre-training (TPP), which introduces an intermediate self-supervised stage for additive PEFT. During this stage, the backbone remains frozen while the target parameters are optimized on the downstream training images through a pretext task. The learned parameters are then used to initialize supervised PEFT. TPP can be integrated with different backbones, pretext tasks, and additive PEFT methods without modifying their inference-time architectures. We evaluate TPP on ten public datasets spanning five imaging modalities and both classification and segmentation tasks. TPP improves most evaluated PEFT-method and dataset combinations, while its effectiveness depends on data alignment, target-data availability, and compatibility between the pretext objective and PEFT architecture. Code will be released at: https://github.com/xl-lei/TPP.

articles.title: Cross-modality Knowledge Transfer Between fMRI and EEG for Improved Single-modality Alzheimer's Disease Diagnosis.
articles.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) disrupts brain function in both spatial organization and temporal dynamics, which can be characterized by complementary fMRI and EEG measurements. In particular, fMRI provides higher spatial resolution to characterize multi-scale functional organization of brain networks, whereas EEG offers higher temporal resolution to capture dynamic neural activities across frequency bands. Thus, integrating the two modalities can characterize AD-related spatiotemporal disruptions more comprehensively than either modality alone. However, it is impractical to acquire paired fMRI and EEG data in real-world applications. To address this problem, we propose the fMRI-EEG Knowledge Transfer Network (FE-KTNet) to learn spatiotemporal representations from paired data and then transfer them back to modality-specific models through three stages. Specifically, in Stage 1, it learns modality-specific representations from fMRI and EEG FCNs, emphasizing multi-scale network organization for fMRI and frequency-specific electrophysiological coupling for EEG. Building on these representations, in Stage 2, it performs scale-wise bidirectional cross-modality fusion to integrate complementary information into fused multi-scale spatiotemporal representations. Finally, in Stage 3, it transfers the fused representations back to each modality-specific encoder through scale-wise feature alignment and logit-level knowledge distillation. We evaluate FE-KTNet on 14 multicenter datasets comprising 2,766 fMRI subjects and 1,842 EEG subjects, covering AD-NC, MCI-NC, and AD-MCI classifications. Compared with the corresponding baseline models, FE-KTNet increases fMRI-only and EEG-only accuracy by 3.4% and 6.1% for AD-NC classification, 5.2% and 8.0% for MCI-NC classification, and 3.5% and 7.1% for AD-MCI classification, respectively, and achieves the best overall performance among all evaluated methods. Our code is available at GitHub Repository.

articles.title: Improved detection of central vein sign in multiple sclerosis using optimized susceptibility weighted imaging at 3 Tesla.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVES: The central vein sign (CVS) is a novel diagnostic imaging biomarker that improves differentiation of white matter lesions (WMLs) caused by multiple sclerosis (MS) and radiological mimics. While susceptibility-weighted imaging (SWI) is widely available for visualizing venous structures, standard SWI protocols are not optimized for standalone CVS detection and require T2-FLAIR images to co-localize T2-hyperintense WMLs. This study evaluated whether an optimized SWI protocol improves CVS detection and reader confidence at 3 T. MATERIALS AND METHODS: Seventeen patients with a clinical diagnosis of MS were scanned on a 3 T MRI scanner using a standard SWI and an optimized SWI acquired with a lower flip angle (FA = 5°). Two radiologists, blinded to the SWI imaging protocols, evaluated the presence of CVS and their confidence levels. Subsequent subject-level analysis was performed to assess the positive detection rate for MS using the "Select-6" rule. RESULTS: Optimized SWI detected all CVS+ lesions identified by standard SWI plus 33 additional lesions (105 vs. 72). Optimized SWI detected more CVS+ lesions than standard SWI in 14/17 participants, with a higher median number of CVS+ lesions detected per participant (7.0 vs. 4.0; p < 0.001). Optimized SWI also increased high-confidence CVS+ classification compared with standard SWI (p = 0.006). Positive detection rate for MS using Select-6 increased from 41.2% with standard SWI to 82.4% with optimized SWI (p = 0.016). CONCLUSION: This feasibility study demonstrates that acquiring SWI with a lower FA at 3 T significantly improves CVS detection, reader confidence, and positive detection rate for MS. KEY POINTS: Question Standard SWI can visualize venous structures at 3 T, but provides limited lesion conspicuity, which prevents standalone detection of the central vein sign (CVS). Findings Optimized SWI with a low flip angle detects more CVS-positive lesions, increases high-confidence CVS classification, and improves MS detection rate using the Select-6 rule. Clinical relevance Optimized SWI improves CVS visibility and rater confidence without increasing scan time, providing a simple technical optimization for assessment of CVS at 3 T.

Generative Adversarial Networks in Medical Imaging: A Scoping Review of Applications, Translational Readiness, and Evidence Gaps.
articles.abstract: This scoping review maps the recent applications of generative adversarial network (GAN)-based methods in medical imaging from 2021 to 2025. The aim was to provide an evidence map of recent original studies, focusing on methodological categories, imaging modalities, anatomical targets, application domains, translational-readiness evidence, and trustworthiness gaps. The scoping review was conducted and reported in accordance with the PRISMA extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR). PubMed, Scopus, and IEEE Xplore were searched, supplemented by manual screening of reference lists and related articles. Original full-text articles published in English between 2021 and 2025 were eligible if they used adversarially trained GAN-based methods for medical imaging tasks. A total of 112 studies were included after duplicate removal and two-stage screening. GAN-based methods were most often applied to disease diagnosis support, image reconstruction, image quality enhancement, cross-modality translation, anatomical segmentation, and training data expansion. Evidence reporting differed substantially across the five assessed domains. External validation was clearly reported in 17 studies (15.2%), prospective evaluation in 2 (1.8%), and clinical workflow integration in 3 (2.7%). Privacy assessment was not clearly reported in any study, with only one (0.9%) partially addressing this domain. In contrast, hallucination or failure analysis was clearly reported in 32 studies (28.6%) and partially reported in 74 (66.1%). These findings indicate widespread technical experimentation but uneven documentation of evidence relevant to clinical translation. Further external and prospective evaluation, explicit privacy assessment, more comprehensive failure analysis, and clinician-centered workflow studies are needed to support the responsible clinical implementation of GAN-based medical imaging methods.

articles.title: Penile inversion vaginoplasty: embryologic map, institutional technique, expected neoanatomy, and imaging of complications.
articles.abstract: It is important to understand the surgical steps involved in the creation of the external genitalia to effectively evaluate pelvic imaging in transgender individuals after penile inversion vaginoplasty (PIV). This review provides an overview of PIV, correlates neoanatomy with imaging, and discusses imaging evaluation of postoperative complications to guide clinical practice. During embryonic development of external genitalia, the genital tubercle differentiates into the glans penis and the clitoris in the male and female, respectively. The urogenital sinus differentiates into the lining of the male urethra and the lining of the vestibule in females. Importantly, embryologic homology provides a framework for understanding postoperative neoanatomy. Our institutional approach to PIV surgery utilizes the glans penis to construct the neoclitoris, the lining of the urethra to construct the neovestibule, and the penile and scrotal skin to line the neovagina. After surgery, contrast-enhanced CT is generally the first-line imaging modality for suspected acute deep postoperative complications, while MRI is preferred for detailed evaluation of neoanatomy and chronic postoperative complications. Correlating embryologic development, surgical technique, and imaging may improve clinician understanding of neoanatomy after PIV. This may facilitate accurate imaging evaluation of pelvic pathology in transgender individuals after PIV and promote timely diagnosis.

articles.title: Imaging evaluation of pediatric acquired hearing loss.
articles.abstract: Pediatric acquired hearing loss represents a clinical challenge, requiring prompt diagnosis in order to optimize normal language and psychosocial development. This review outlines a practical imaging framework categorizing acquired hearing loss etiologies into opacified and aerated middle ears. High-resolution computed tomography (CT) is the gold standard for delineating osseous anatomy, including ossicular discontinuity, fractures, and congenital or acquired bone erosion. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) provides soft-tissue characterization, and can evaluate labyrinth contents, cranial nerves, and for intracranial complications; non-echo-planar diffusion-weighted imaging (non-EPI DWI) can help to identify cholesteatomas. By leveraging these complementary modalities, radiologists can establish a precise diagnostic roadmap to guide clinical management and surgical intervention.

articles.title: Imaging of congenital sensorineural hearing loss: a review of syndromic and non-syndromic causes.
articles.abstract: Congenital sensorineural hearing loss (cSNHL) has been increasingly recognized given improvements in prenatal and childhood screening efforts. Etiologies vary widely with a growing body of literature continuing to uncover underlying risk factors and associated syndromes. cSNHL results in significant morbidity with the potential to impair language and social development. Imaging is an integral part of the clinical and potential presurgical assessment for these children. Thus, it is essential for radiologists to be familiar with normal inner ear anatomy, inner ear malformations, and syndromic/genetic etiologies of sensorineural hearing loss.

articles.title: From Salience to Attentional Displacement in AI-assisted Diagnosis.
Development of RF Probes and Preamplifiers for MRI at Low Fields.
articles.abstract: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) systems operating at low magnetic fields (   B 0  ≲ 0 . 25   T) have experienced renewed interest due to the emergence of portable, point-of-care (POC) scanners, and new approaches to mitigating the intrinsically lower signal-to-noise ratios (SNR). The performance of radiofrequency (RF) components is a large factor in determining overall system sensitivity. In contrast to conventional MRI, at higher fields where SNR is typically sample-noise dominated, many low field (LF) systems operate in a coil-noise dominated regime, requiring careful optimization of RF coil design, conductor losses, and receiver electronics. This manuscript surveys RF coil technologies and associated hardware considerations for MRI systems operating below approximately 0.18T, within the range that we designate as low field in this manuscript (0-250 mT). We begin by revisiting early low-field imaging systems and the historical development of RF coil architectures for large-volume imaging. The fundamental noise mechanisms governing low-frequency MR detection are then examined, including Johnson noise in conductors, sample-induced losses, receiver noise figure, and electromagnetic interference (EMI). Design strategies for improving sensitivity are discussed, including conductor optimization (e.g., Litz wire), coil geometry selection such as solenoidal and saddle configurations, and methods for managing coil bandwidth and quality factor. Recent developments in transmit-receive switching, preamplifier design, EMI mitigation, and coil-preamplifier co-design are also reviewed. Finally, we highlight emerging directions for RF hardware development in low-field MRI, including RF coils for encoding, multi-element receive arrays for parallel imaging, and receiver architectures inspired by related modalities such as magnetic particle imaging and ultrasound. Continued advances in RF coil and receiver-chain design will be essential for improving sensitivity and enabling low-field MRI systems for clinical and research applications.

articles.title: Radiomics-Based Differentiation of Enchondroma from Atypical Cartilaginous Tumour and Chondrosarcoma: A Systematic Review and Appraisal.
articles.abstract: The objective was to systematically review radiomics models that differentiate enchondroma from atypical cartilaginous tumour (ACT) or chondrosarcoma and to appraise their methodological quality and readiness for clinical use. PubMed, Embase, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials and Scopus were searched from inception to 24 October 2026 for radiomic, machine learning or deep learning models applied to CT, MRI, radiography or bone SPECT/CT (PROSPERO registration number withheld for blinded review). Performance was synthesised descriptively, not pooled. Quality was appraised with PROBAST + AI, TRIPOD + AI, the Radiomics Quality Score and METRICS. Fourteen reports representing 13 retrospective cohorts (1447 participants, including 79 control scans) were included; two probably overlapping reports were counted once. Eight cohorts used MRI, three CT, one both and one bone SPECT/CT; three reports evaluated deep learning. Eight reports supplied an exact or derivable 2 × 2 table for one of two clinical targets. Sensitivity ranged from 0.800 to 0.935 and specificity from 0.727 to 1.000; preferred areas under the curve (AUC) ranged from 0.801 to 1.000. Development quality concern was high in all reports, and all 22 diagnostic evaluation datasets had high risk of bias. One study used geographically external validation; none was prospective or reported decision curve analysis. Median complete TRIPOD + AI reporting was 48.3%. Reported discrimination was promising but methodologically preliminary and does not establish clinical usefulness; prospective assessment and independent multicentre external validation are required.

articles.title: Intelligent Prediction of WHO/ISUP Grade in Clear-Cell Renal Cell Carcinoma Using CT-Based Fusion Delta Features: A Multicenter Study with Biological Interpretability Exploration.
articles.abstract: RATIONALE AND OBJECTIVES: Our study aimed to develop a delta deep learning radiomics model for predicting World Health Organization/International Society of Urological Pathology (WHO/ISUP) grade in clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC) and to find relevant biomarkers and explore the potential biological mechanisms. MATERIAL AND METHODS: This multicenter cohort of 754 patients with ccRCC from five hospitals was split into training and internal validation cohorts in a 7:3 ratio, along with an external validation cohort (n=221) from three other hospitals. Radiomics and deep learning features were extracted from the tumor regions on multiphase contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT). Delta features were calculated as the absolute differences between features from different imaging phases. The selected features were used to develop delta deep learning radiomics signatures using different classifiers. The diagnostic performance in each model was assessed. Furthermore, gene expression profiling was conducted to for exploratory analysis of biological correlates associated with the model's grade predictions. RESULTS: The delta model achieved AUCs of 0.736 (95% CI 0.671-0.801) and 0.701 (95% CI 0.635-0.768) in the internal and external validation cohorts, respectively, which were numerically higher than those of the original model based on traditional deep learning radiomics features and demographic baseline clinical model. Additionally, the delta model demonstrated good calibration and a higher net benefit. Bioinformatics and multiomics analysis revealed that high-grade risk-related differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were associated with inflammation-related pathways, providing preliminary exploratory biological insights into the model's predictions. CONCLUSION: The delta model demonstrated promising performance in WHO/ISUP grade. DEGs in predicted high-grade ccRCC were associated with inflammation-related pathways.

articles.title: Computed tomography-guided percutaneous cryoablation for pediatric osteoid osteoma: clinical success and safety.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Percutaneous thermal ablation has replaced surgery as first-line treatment for osteoid osteoma in many centers. Radiofrequency ablation is the most widely reported technique, whereas cryoablation is an alternative thermal ablation technique. Pediatric data on cryoablation for osteoid osteoma remain limited. OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the clinical and technical success of CT-guided percutaneous cryoablation for osteoid osteoma in children and adolescents. Safety and radiation exposure were assessed as secondary procedural outcomes. MATERIALS AND METHODS: This retrospective single-center study included 18 consecutive patients (10 males; median age 13.5 years, range 6-17) who underwent CT-guided cryoablation between December 2022 and May 2025. Clinical success at 1 month and technical success were the main outcomes. Society of Interventional Radiology (SIR)-classified adverse events, pain evolution, analgesic use, procedure duration, and dose-length product were recorded as secondary outcomes. Pain was assessed using the numeric rating scale (NRS). RESULTS: Technical success was achieved in all procedures (18/18). Clinical success was achieved in all patients by the 1-month clinical follow-up. Median time to complete pain relief was 1 day (interquartile range, 1-2 days); 13/18 patients were pain-free within 24 h, all patients were pain-free within 14 days, and all had discontinued analgesics at 1 month. No SIR-classified procedure-related adverse event was observed in this cohort. Median dose-length product was 158 mGy·cm (interquartile range, 100-300). CONCLUSION: CT-guided cryoablation achieved technical success and complete clinical success at 1 month in this pediatric osteoid osteoma cohort, with rapid pain relief, discontinuation of analgesics, and no SIR-classified procedure-related adverse event observed.

articles.title: Feasibility of prior-informed domain-based electrical impedance tomography for deep tissue thermometry: Phantom experiments and computed tomography-derived numerical simulations.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Accurate monitoring of deep tissue temperature is important during hyperthermia treatment. Because the electrical conductivity of biological tissue generally increases with temperature, Electrical Impedance Tomography (EIT) may provide a non-invasive approach for estimating temperature changes in deep tissue. PURPOSE: This study aimed to evaluate a domain-based EIT thermometry framework for quantitative temperature estimation in electrically heterogeneous settings composed of piecewise homogeneous domains, where conventional voxel-based EIT reconstruction is limited by the ill-posed inverse problem and inaccurate separation of domain-level conductivity changes. METHODS: Simulation and phantom studies were performed. In the simulation study, reconstruction performance was evaluated using reconstruction error and stability. In the phantom experiments, performance was evaluated using the mean and maximum absolute temperature errors over reconstructed frames by comparing sensor-measured temperatures with EIT-based estimates. An anatomically realistic model was additionally constructed from a single respiratory phase of one patient computed tomography (CT) dataset, and nine anatomical subdomains were reconstructed under target-centered and external-entry heating scenarios. RESULTS: In the simulation study, the proposed domain-based reconstruction yielded the lowest reconstruction error across the evaluated noise conditions. In phantom experiments, it showed close agreement with direct measurements under all tested conditions. The average conductivity reconstruction error in the homogeneous phantom was 0.29%, while the mean absolute temperature errors in the multi-domain phantoms ranged from 0.22°C to 0.71°C. In pooled phantom comparisons, the proposed method showed mean and maximum absolute temperature errors of 0.44 ± 0.31°C and 0.91 ± 0.77°C, respectively. In the CT-derived model, the mean absolute temperature errors were 0.50°C and 1.43°C for the target-centered and external-entry scenarios, compared with 1.21-1.25°C and 2.60-2.67°C for the benchmark methods, respectively, and the location of the hottest region was preserved in both scenarios. CONCLUSION: The proposed domain-based EIT thermometry demonstrated feasibility in phantom experiments and a CT-derived anatomical model, establishing a foundation for its potential application as a non-invasive temperature monitoring approach.

articles.title: Association between HER2 expression levels and sonographic features in triple-negative breast cancer.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To investigate the association between HER2 expression levels and sonographic characteristics in patients with triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC). METHODS: A retrospective analysis was performed on 173 patients with pathologically confirmed TNBC. Based on HER2 immunohistochemistry (IHC) results, patients were classified into three groups: HER2-negative (IHC 0), HER2-low (IHC 1+), and HER2-low (IHC 2 + without amplification as determined by fluorescence in situ hybridization [FISH]). Sonographic features-including tumor shape, orientation, internal echogenicity, margin, posterior acoustic features, and presence of calcification-as well as lymph node metastasis status were compared across the groups. RESULTS: With increasing HER2 expression levels, tumors were more likely to exhibit an irregular shape (p < 0.001), non-circumscribed margins (p = 0.009), reduced incidence of posterior acoustic enhancement (p = 0.004), and higher frequency of calcification (p = 0.026). No significant differences were observed in tumor orientation or internal echogenicity among the groups (p > 0.05). The rate of lymph node metastasis did not differ significantly across the three groups (p = 0.233). CONCLUSION: HER2 expression level is associated with specific sonographic features in TNBC, with higher expression correlating with more suspicious ultrasound characteristics. Although a trend toward increased lymph node metastasis was noted in the HER2-low (IHC 2+) group, this difference was not statistically significant, warranting further investigation.

articles.title: Evaluation of lesion and neoadjuvant treatment response using low-keV dual-energy CT in breast cancer.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Exploring the capacity of detecting breast cancer lesion on different monoenergetic images (MEIs) and predicting NAT response using quantitative parameters derived from DECT. METHODS: This retrospective study enrolled patients with invasive breast cancer who received NAT followed by surgery. Meanwhile, all participants underwent chest DECT and breast MRI before and after NAT. The first end was to assess different MEIs for detecting breast lesion using objective and subjective measurements. The second end was to establish model for predicting pCR using quantitative parameters, and compare the model with visual MRI-rCR. The Kaplan-Meier method was used to analyze prognosis. RESULTS: 199 women with breast cancer were included (median age, 50 years). 52 (26.13%) achieved pCR and 147 (73.87%) were non-pCR after NAT. Low keV MEI had optimal performance to characterize lesion, especially on 40 keV MEI at venous phase (CNR: 6.55, SNR: 7.23, Likert score: 5; all p < 0.001). The multivariable regression showed HER2 positivity (OR, 0.155; 95% CI: 0.061-0.393; p < 0.001) and CT value on 40 keV MEI at venous phase (OR, 1.067; 95% CI: 1.020-1.117; p = 0.005) were independently associated with pCR. The established combined model yielded an AUC of 0.900 (95% CI: 0.856-0.944) when assessed on the full study cohort, beyond the MRI-rCR (AUC, 0.900 vs. 0.782; p = 0.003). The model also showed a nominally significant association with disease-free survival (DFS) on the whole dataset (log-rank, p = 0.046). CONCLUSIONS: MEI with low keV significantly improved visualization of breast cancer. Quantitative parameters derived from 40 keV MEI demonstrated superior value for assessing NAT response and prognosis compared to MRI-rCR. QUESTION: Dual-energy CT has been used for diagnosis of breast lesion. However, the predictive performance to evaluate neoadjuvant treatment response remains unexplored in breast cancer. FINDINGS: Monoenergetic images (MEIs) with low keV has optimal performance for visualization of breast cancer and its quantitative parameters can identify NAT response and prognosis. CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Low keV MEI effectively visualizes breast cancer as a complementary examination. Its quantitative parameters at 40 keV MEI demonstrated superior value for assessing NAT response and prognosis compared to MRI-rCR so as to assist clinical strategies. CLINICAL TRIAL REGISTRATION: Not applicable.

articles.title: Fast Voxelwise SNR Estimation for Iterative MRI Reconstructions.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: To develop a fast, general-purpose framework for voxelwise noise characterization in iterative MRI reconstructions, recovering the image-domain noise variance, the primary quantity from which SNR, g  -factor, and related image-quality metrics are derived. The framework addresses both the intractability of closed-form formulas beyond Cartesian sampling and the long runtime of pseudo multiple replica (PMR). METHODS: A stochastic noise estimator is proposed that operates in the image domain by Probing the Image-space noise COvariance matrix (PICO) with random probe images. Complex random-phase probes attain minimum kurtosis and reduce estimator variance in the tested reconstruction. PICO was validated against analytical benchmarks and PMR references using Cartesian knee data ( R = 2  ), physical brain phantom data ( R = 2 , 3 , 4  ), in vivo non-Cartesian brain data ( R = 2  ), and compressed-sensing knee reconstructions ( R = 2  ). RESULTS: In Cartesian reconstructions, PICO accurately reproduced analytical SENSE g  -factor maps. In non-Cartesian reconstructions, it achieved 1 %  g  -factor NRMSE ≈ 11 . 9 ×  faster than PMR in a phantom and ≈ 2 . 81 ×  faster in vivo, with the efficiency advantage persisting at higher acceleration. For compressed sensing, the Jacobian-based estimator produced noise maps consistent with PMR and computed them 1 . 84 ×  faster at equal sample counts. Agreement worsened at large added-noise amplitudes and moderate TV strengths. CONCLUSION: PICO targets the exact covariance of fixed linear reconstructions and a first-order covariance for nonlinear reconstructions, providing a computationally efficient alternative to PMR. By reusing existing reconstruction primitives, it could help incorporate voxelwise noise maps into reconstruction workflows.

articles.title: Rigid Motion Estimation Using Accelerated Coordinate Descent (REACT) for MR Imaging.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: To develop a computationally viable autofocus method for estimating 3D rigid motion in MR imaging. THEORY AND METHODS: The proposed method, REACT, assumes a piecewise-constant motion trajectory and estimates the rigid motion parameters of individual temporal segments by optimizing an image-quality metric. Coordinate descent is adopted to decompose the high-dimensional optimization problem into a series of subproblems, each updating the motion parameters of a single temporal segment. The cost function of each subproblem is assumed to be approximately locally convex under suitable acquisition conditions. Each subproblem is then solved using a derivative-free solver, thereby avoiding an exhaustive grid search. Numerical simulations investigated the local convexity assumption and data acquisition requirements. REACT was evaluated for respiratory motion correction on in vivo free-breathing coronary MR angiography datasets. Coronary artery sharpness was quantified using unbounded image edge profile acutance (u-IEPA). RESULTS: In numerical simulations, the objective surfaces of the subproblems were approximately locally convex when the current motion estimate was sufficiently close to the desired solution, and REACT required the data collected within each temporal segment to be sufficiently distributed across k  -space. In the in vivo study, REACT yielded higher u-IEPA for both the left anterior descending artery (LAD) and the right coronary artery than did a conventional translational motion-estimation method using image-based navigators. REACT also yielded higher u-IEPA for the LAD than did a conventional autofocus nonrigid motion correction method. CONCLUSION: This study demonstrates the feasibility of coordinate descent for autofocus motion correction in MR imaging.

articles.title: Optimal RF Phase Modulation for Improved Magnetic Resonance Fingerprinting T2 Encoding and Efficiency.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: To improve magnetic resonance fingerprinting (MRF) T2 encoding by combining phase-based T2 encoding with optimal experiment design. METHODS: Six hundred-timepoint MRF sequences with jointly optimized flip angle (FA) and quadratic RF phase increment schedules were generated by minimizing their Cramér-Rao Lower Bound for tissue dependent sets of T1 and T2. Sequences were optimized for 3T and 0.55T brain MRF and 0.55T prostate MRF and compared against FA-only optimized and unoptimized (600- and 1000-timepoint) sequences. Accuracy and precision were first evaluated using Monte-Carlo Bloch simulations in a digital phantom. Additional simulations identified a spiral interleaf ordering which minimized aliasing artifacts under phase modulation. A T1/T2 phantom was then used to validate simulation results. In vivo performance was assessed in nine healthy subjects, where precision was measured using bootstrap Monte-Carlo experiments with 50 pseudo-replicas. RESULTS: Jointly optimized sequences were found to produce T2 maps with significantly greater accuracy and precision than unoptimized and FA-only optimized sequences in simulation and phantom experiments (p < 0.001). A Step 5 (37.5° between timepoints) spiral interleaf ordering minimized aliasing under phase modulation, while maintaining comparable performance without. In vivo testing in the brain and prostate revealed higher T2 values, reduced T2 coefficients of variation, and lower B1 + sensitivity than unoptimized and FA-only optimized sequence variants. CONCLUSION: Simulation, phantom, and in vivo studies demonstrate that optimized RF phase modulation improves MRF T2 encoding compared to unoptimized and FA-only optimized sequences, enabling shorter exams and greater T2 precision in the brain and pelvis at 3T and 0.55T.

articles.title: An On-Premise, Open-Weights Vision-Language Pipeline for Burned-In PHI Removal: Detection, Decision, and Image Degradation on MIDI-B.
articles.abstract: Burned-in protected health information (PHI) in DICOM pixel data blocks multi-site imaging research, and better recognition is assumed to be the route to removal. We asked whether detection or the PHI decision limits removal. A layered pixel pipeline built on Florence-2 OCR was evaluated on MIDI-B with the CBIIT validation script. Against the answer key's OCR-independent coordinates, two controlled arms swapped the engine with the decision fixed, then varied the decision over detections. A nine-condition degradation sweep ran to redaction, with Wilson intervals and exact McNemar tests. On clean images, a 0.23 B vision-language model and a CNN OCR at library defaults detected 34/35 and 35/35 regions, flagged the same 10/35 with the decision fixed, and removed the same 33/35. Over fixed detections, Microsoft Presidio flagged 12/35 and a generic rule set 10/35, as 25 of 35 regions are unpatterned markers; redacting every detection reached 35/35, so both shipped misses were decision misses. Under degradation, both engines detected the text in every condition; removal differed most at blur radius 4, 32 versus 26 (p = 0.07), where the CNN OCR misread short markers (exact match 17/25 versus 10/25). An earlier-reported collapse to 18/35 came from a confidence floor in our harness. The strict profile scored 33/35 at 86.7% series accuracy, and the retain profile 32/35 at 97.6%. Removal on clean text is limited by the PHI decision, not the detector. Under synthetic degradation, the engines differ in transcribing short strings, not in detecting them, by a margin this sample cannot resolve. Results are benchmark- and engine-specific.

articles.title: On-Premises Open-Weight Large Language Models for Classifying Epilepsy Brain MRI Reports: A Retrospective Study.
articles.abstract: Free-text reports limit the use of imaging data for research cohort screening. This study evaluated whether locally deployed open-weight large language models (LLMs) can classify brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) reports in epilepsy without external data transfer, and which forms of domain knowledge improve classification. In this single-center retrospective study, 1210 epilepsy-protocol brain MRI reports were labeled by a board-certified neuroradiologist for abnormality status and primary imaging finding (eight classes). A held-out test set of 206 reports was classified by a biomedical (OpenBioLLM-8B) and a general-purpose (Qwen3.5-9B) LLM on a single 24-GB graphics processing unit, with and without a rule set and example retrieval, and compared with a fine-tuned radiology-specific BERT model, an independent neuroradiology fellow, and a same-base control model. The primary outcome was the macro-averaged F1 score for the primary finding. Without task-specific training, the general-purpose model achieved a finding macro-F1 of 0.63 (95% confidence interval (CI), 0.53-0.70), comparable to the fine-tuned BERT model (0.59; difference, - 0.04; 95% CI, - 0.13 to 0.07) and to inter-reader agreement (0.61; κ = 0.59). A rule set stating institutional category definitions improved the biomedical model (difference, 0.23; 95% CI, 0.11-0.33) without significantly reducing performance in any model, whereas biomedical fine-tuning conferred no advantage over the control model and example retrieval did not help. Residual errors concentrated where the readers disagreed. Locally deployed LLMs performed comparably to inter-reader agreement, which may support human-verified cohort screening; in this institution-specific task, explicit category definitions were more useful than biomedical specialization.

articles.title: The Additive Value of 18F-PSMA-1007 PET/CT in Assessing Outcomes in Patients with Biochemical Recurrence After Radical Prostatectomy.
articles.abstract: RATIONALE AND OBJECTIVES: In recent studies, prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA) positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PET/CT) has shown accuracy in restaging patients with biochemical recurrence (BCR). Here, we aim to evaluate the impact of ¹⁸F-PSMA-1007 PET/CT-guided treatment escalation (GTE) on clinical outcomes and validate an integrated prognostic model for biochemical progression-free survival (bPFS). MATERIALS AND METHODS: This retrospective study included patients who underwent 18F-PSMA-1007 PET/CT for BCR between April 2019 and October 2024. We employed Kaplan-Meier analysis to assess and compare the prognostic value of PSMA PET/CT-GTE across patient subgroups. Univariate and multivariate Cox analyses identified predictors of bPFS. These were used to construct a multimodal nomogram, assessed via calibration plots and time-dependent ROC curves. RESULTS: A total of 303 patients were randomly split into a training set (n = 223) and a test set (n = 80) in a 7:3 ratio. Kaplan-Meier analysis showed significantly different bPFS with or without PSMA PET/CT-GTE in the bone metastasis (P = .024), local recurrence (P = .040), and mixed metastasis groups (P = .029). Multivariate COX regression analysis identified ISUP grade, PSMA PET/CT-GTE, and recurrence locations as independent predictors of bPFS. The multimodal nomogram demonstrated good discrimination (C-index 0.728 in the training set) and calibration, with time-dependent AUCs ranging from 0.755 to 0.841 for predicting 1-, 2-, and 3-year bPFS in the training set. CONCLUSION: PSMA PET/CT-GTE is linked to prolonged bPFS in BCR patients after RP. A model combining PSMA PET/CT-GTE, recurrence locations on PSMA PET/CT, and ISUP grade demonstrate good predictive performance for bPFS.

articles.title: Integrating Intratumoral and Peritumoral Features via a Cross-Attention Transformer on Super-resolution MRI for Glioblastoma Survival Risk Stratification: A Multicenter Study.
articles.abstract: RATIONALE AND OBJECTIVES: To develop and validate a Cross-Region Transformer using super-resolution (SR) magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to integrate intratumoral and peritumoral features for overall survival (OS) prediction in glioblastoma. MATERIALS AND METHODS: This multicenter study included 362 patients (training, n = 228; internal test, n = 57; external validation, n = 77). Preoperative contrast-enhanced T1-weighted and T2-weighted MRI underwent generative adversarial network-based SR reconstruction. Intratumoral and 10-mm peritumoral features were extracted using 2.5D convolutional neural networks and fused by asymmetric cross-attention to generate a deep learning-based risk score (DLRS), which was combined with independent clinical factors. Performance was evaluated using C-index, time-dependent receiver operating characteristic analysis, calibration, decision curve analysis, Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping, and SHapley Additive exPlanations. RESULTS: The Cross-Region Transformer achieved C-indices of 0.787 (95% confidence interval [CI], 0.734-0.840), 0.711 (95% CI, 0.593-0.829), and 0.726 (95% CI, 0.627-0.826) in the training, internal test, and external validation cohorts, respectively, with numerically higher discrimination than single-region and feature-concatenation models. The combined clinical-DLRS model, incorporating the Stupp regimen, number of lesions, Ki-67 index, and DLRS, achieved corresponding C-indices of 0.836 (95% CI, 0.788-0.884), 0.742 (95% CI, 0.628-0.855), and 0.754 (95% CI, 0.658-0.850). The DLRS significantly stratified OS in external validation (median, 7.5 vs 23.5 months; P < 0.001). Interpretability analyses highlighted enhancing margins within the necrotic core and the intratumoral-peritumoral interface. CONCLUSION: The Cross-Region Transformer integrates complementary intratumoral and peritumoral representations from SR MRI. The resulting interpretable DLRS supports noninvasive survival prediction and risk stratification in glioblastoma.

articles.title: Simultaneous Lymph Node and Vascular Suppression Using Ferumoxytol-Enhanced Magnetic Resonance Neurography.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND AND PURPOSE: Lymph nodes and blood vessels are hyperintense on heavily T2-weighted magnetic resonance neurography (MRN) sequences, potentially confounding nerve visualization. This study prospectively determined a target time between intravenous (IV) administration of ferumoxytol, an ultrasmall superparamagnetic iron oxide nanoparticle, and MR acquisition for simultaneous lymph node (LN) and vascular signal suppression. MATERIALS AND METHODS: Cohort 1 (n=2, age=26.0, 30.6 years, 2 females) received IV ferumoxytol (255 mg) and underwent 5 separate neck MRN exams over a 50-hour time window to determine the target imaging time for LN signal suppression. Subsequently, cohort 2 (n=10, age=26.7 ± 2.7 years, 5 males/5 females) underwent post-ferumoxytol infusion brachial plexus MRN immediately (<1-hour) and at the target time determined from cohort 1 testing. Acquired sequences included 3D, T2-weighted STIR-FSE and double-echo steady state (DESS) at 3T. Two raters selected regions of interest (LN, nerve, artery, vein) to analyze mean contrast ratios (CRs). Two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank tests with Bonferroni correction compared mean LN-to-muscle to nerve-to-muscle CRs (p<0.05 deemed statistically significant). Comparisons were also performed of mean artery-to-muscle and vein-to-muscle CRs against a nominal value of 0.2. Linear mixed effects (LME) models assessed effects of time, rater, subject, weight and anatomical location on mean CRs. RESULTS: Significantly lower mean LN-to-muscle than nerve-to-muscle CRs were observed at the target 15-hour time using STIR-FSE (CR=1.25-1.44 vs. 2.03-2.30) and DESS (CR=0.56-0.57 vs. 1.70-1.99). Mean artery-to-muscle and vein-to-muscle CRs were significantly less than 0.2 on STIR-FSE (CR=0.06-0.13). LME models confirmed decreased mean LN-to-muscle CR on STIR-FSE (by -1.41) and DESS (by -0.87) at 15-hours. CONCLUSIONS: Simultaneous LN and vascular signal suppression was achieved 15 hours post-ferumoxytol infusion on MRN sequences. Concurrent LN and vascular signal suppression may warrant further investigation into the ability to visualize small, difficult-to-assess nerves within the neck and axilla.

articles.title: ASFNR Clinical State-of-Practice in Neuroimaging of Minor Large Vessel Occlusion Stroke.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Minor ischemic stroke (MIS) with anterior large vessel occlusion (LVO) is a distinct stroke subtype in which mild neurological deficits may mask a substantial volume of threatened but salvageable brain tissue. Despite a baseline NIHSS≤5, nearly one-third of patients experience poor functional outcomes, often due to early neurological deterioration (END). CURRENT EVIDENCE AND ONGOING TRIALS: Patients with LVO-MIS were markedly underrepresented in landmark thrombectomy trials, resulting in limited evidence to guide treatment. Retrospective studies have identified imaging biomarkers of END, including proximal occlusion, clot length, collateral status, and perfusion mismatch, but the benefit of endovascular thrombectomy (EVT) remains uncertain. Ongoing randomized controlled trials, including STEP and MOSTE, are expected to define the role of EVT and imaging-based patient selection in this population. PURPOSE: To summarize the current state of neuroimaging in anterior circulation LVO-MIS and provide a practical imaging workflow and reporting checklist for diagnosis, prognostication, and treatment selection. KEY POINTS: CTA remains the primary modality for LVO detection and collateral assessment, while CT and MR perfusion identify salvageable tissue and predict END beyond baseline NIHSS. MRI further refines infarct core, perfusion deficit, and thrombus characterization. Current AI-based LVO detection tools improve stroke triage but require careful human oversight because proximal M2 and non-terminus ICA occlusions may be missed. CONCLUSION: Pending results from ongoing trials, tissue-based imaging with CTA, CT perfusion, and MR perfusion can complement clinical assessment to improve risk stratification and individualized treatment decisions. Advances in quantitative imaging and artificial intelligence are expected to further enable precision imaging-guided management of LVO-MIS.

articles.title: A bridge too far? Is there a positive benefit/risk balance of distal embolic penetration in MMA embolization for cSDHs?
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Middle meningeal artery embolization for chronic subdural hematoma is rapidly expanding in practice, with growing interest in techniques that maximize distal penetration of liquid embolic agents within the meningeal branches to reach the neovascularized hematoma membrane. The clinical significance of distal embolic penetration beyond its radiographic associations has not been fully established, and reports of rare complications associated with more aggressive technique raise safety considerations. This State of Practice examines evidence for distal embolic penetration's clinical benefits, presents a case illustrating a risk associated with this approach, and outlines the evidence needed to determine its benefit/risk balance. METHODS: The authors conducted a narrative review of randomized trials, retrospective studies, and case-based literature on middle meningeal artery embolization, comparing reported embolic penetration/grading frameworks and evidence for their association with radiographic and clinical outcomes, as well as evidence for proximal coil embolization as an alternative approach. We also report a case of inadvertent embolization through an occult middle meningeal artery anastomosis to illustrate a risk of distal embolic penetration. KEY MESSAGE: As practice of middle meningeal artery embolization expands, evidence that maximizing distal liquid embolic penetration improves clinical outcomes beyond radiographic resolution remains limited. This approach may involve rare complications from occult vascular anastomoses not readily identified on preprocedural imaging, although their frequency is unknown. We urge operators to recognize that an unremarkable preprocedural angiogram may not exclude the dangerous anastomoses. Prospective multicenter studies involving both interventional neuroradiologists and endovascular neurosurgeons are needed to correlate 3D embolic distribution patterns with clinical outcomes, alongside randomized trials comparing distal and proximal embolization approaches using clinically meaningful endpoints.

articles.title: Predictors of radiation-induced lymphopenia in NSCLC: blood and bone marrow dose during chemoradiotherapy.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: Radiation-induced lymphopenia (RIL) is a significant complication for patients with non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) undergoing radiotherapy, particularly as immunotherapy becomes increasingly integral to treatment. Understanding the predictors and mechanisms underlying RIL will support and help direct efforts to preserve anti-tumor immunity and optimizing therapeutic outcomes. METHODS: This study assessed the relationship between radiation dose to the blood and bone marrow and the development and recovery of lymphopenia in two (training and validation) cohorts, 134 patients in total, with NSCLC treated with either proton (PSPT) or photon-based chemoradiotherapy (CRT) between June 2009 and March 2014. Compartmental blood flow models and automatic organ segmentation were used to quantify radiation doses to circulating blood, large vessels and proliferating bone marrow. Multivariable logistic regression was performed to identify significant predictors of severe lymphopenia within 2 months from CRT start and its recovery. RESULTS: We found that both the generalized equivalent uniform dose (gEUD) to blood and baseline absolute lymphocyte count (ALC) were significant predictors of grade 4 lymphopenia. The discriminative ability (measured by AUC) for blood dose gEUD peaked around negative alpha values, suggesting that low-dose contributions to the blood pool are most relevant for predicting lymphopenia risk. Despite proton therapy delivering mean blood doses lower by 12.1% (p = 0.006) compared to photon therapy, there were no significant differences in nadir lymphocyte counts between the modalities. Bone marrow dose was only weakly correlated with lymphocyte nadir and showed no association with lymphocyte recovery after treatment. CONCLUSION: Our findings demonstrate that radiation dose to circulating blood is a significant predictor of radiation-induced lymphopenia in NSCLC patients. Despite the observed correlations, these findings suggest that optimizing radiation dose to the blood alone may not be the most effective strategy for reducing lymphopenia.

articles.title: Safety and Feasibility of Percutaneous Microwave Ablation of Liver Tumors in Patients with Presumed Colonized Biliary Systems: A Single-Institution Retrospective Study.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: To evaluate the safety and feasibility of percutaneous microwave ablation of liver tumors in patients with prior biliary intervention. We hypothesized that microwave ablation could be performed in this population with an acceptable rate of infectious adverse events (AEs), despite the loss of a competent sphincter of Oddi. MATERIALS AND METHODS: This retrospective study examined all patients at a single institution who underwent liver microwave ablation following a prior biliary intervention resulting in an incompetent or absent sphincter of Oddi. Baseline patient and procedure characteristics, and the prevalence and management of any subsequent infectious AEs, were reviewed. RESULTS: A total of 44 microwave ablation sessions were performed in 24 patients targeting 64 lesions. The technical success rate was 100%. Postprocedural oral antibiotics were prescribed after 36 of 44 sessions. Four hepatic abscesses and one case of cholangitic sepsis occurred after ablation, representing 11.4% of ablation sessions (5 of 44) and 20.8% of patients (5 of 24). All infections were successfully treated. Median overall survival for the entire cohort was 33.5 months. No patient or procedure factor was significantly associated with infectious AEs. Streptococcus viridans, a rarely reported organism in this setting, was isolated from 60% (3 of 5) of patients who developed infectious AEs. CONCLUSION: Microwave ablation was feasible in patients with prior biliary intervention, with high technical success and a higher but acceptable risk of infectious AEs, all of which were successfully treated. These findings support microwave ablation as a valuable modality in this patient population.

articles.title: Microwave Ablation in the Colonized Biliary Tree: Revisiting Liver Thermal Ablation in Patients With Altered Biliary Anatomy.
Diagnostic performance and interobserver agreement of MRI for pancreatic cystic lesions: a multi-reader study with surgical histopathologic correlation.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: To determine the diagnostic performance and interobserver agreement of MRI for differentiating mucinous from non-mucinous pancreatic cystic lesions (PCLs) and identifying advanced neoplasia using surgical pathology as the reference standard. METHODS: This retrospective single-center study included surgically resected PCLs with preoperative MRI (2019-2025). Three independent readers blindly assessed cyst subtype and imaging features, including worrisome features (WF) and high-risk stigmata (HRS) according to the 2024 Kyoto guideline. Consensus interpretation was established with a fourth senior abdominal radiologist. Diagnostic performance for mucinous lesion characterization and advanced neoplasia (high-grade dysplasia and invasive carcinoma) was evaluated. Interobserver agreement was assessed using Fleiss κ and Gwet AC1. Logistic regression and ROC analyses identified imaging predictors of advanced neoplasia. RESULTS: A total of 85 patients were included (mean age, 66.8 ± 12.5 years; 50.6 % female). At pathology, 70/85 lesions (82.4 %) were mucinous and 23/85 (27.1 %) represented advanced neoplasia, including 21 high-grade dysplasia and two IPMN-derived PDAC. MRI consensus interpretation achieved 100 % sensitivity, 80 % specificity, and 96.5 % accuracy for identifying mucinous lesions. MRI demonstrated 52.2 % sensitivity and 67.7 % specificity for advanced neoplasia using WF or HRS, whereas HRS alone improved specificity (95.2 %) at the expense of sensitivity (21.7 %). All readers correctly identified both cases of IPMN-derived PDAC. Interobserver agreement for cyst subtype classification was fair by Fleiss κ but substantial by Gwet AC1, whereas agreement for detecting advanced neoplasia was moderate. Main pancreatic duct diameter independently predicted advanced neoplasia (OR, 1.18; 95 % CI, 1.01-1.38; p = 0.042) and outperformed cyst size (AUC, 0.69 vs 0.56). CONCLUSION: In this surgically selected cohort, consensus MRI differentiates mucinous from nonmucinous PCLs with high sensitivity. Detection of advanced neoplasia, particularly noninvasive high-grade dysplasia, remains challenging because of overlap with low-grade lesions. Fair-to-moderate interobserver agreement highlights the challenges of MRI-based risk stratification. The surgically selected cohort provides histopathologic confirmation but should be considered when interpreting performance estimates in the broader surveillance population.

articles.title: Performance gaps across training, internal testing, and external testing in radiomics models: A meta-research study.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To quantify changes in radiomics model discrimination across training, internal testing, and external testing and assess whether external validation indicates preservation of performance. METHODS: This protocol-guided meta-research study included 2023-2025 radiomics studies reporting training, internal-test, and external-test area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) values for binary models. PubMed/MEDLINE records were selected by randomized quota sampling. Within-study training-to-internal, training-to-external, and internal-to-external AUC gaps were calculated. Equal-weight Wilcoxon signed-rank tests were primary analyses, with paired t tests as secondary analyses. Point estimates defined gap magnitude, and reconstructed approximate 95% confidence intervals described study-level uncertainty. Post hoc inverse-variance random-effects analyses assessed robustness to precision. Additional post hoc sensitivity analyses assessed robustness to external-validation design and external-test data use in harmonization. Exploratory meta-regressions examined associations between training sample size and performance gaps. RESULTS: Forty-nine studies were included. Median AUC declined from 0.920 in training cohorts to 0.882 in internal-test cohorts and 0.860 in external-test cohorts. The training-to-external gap was largest: median, 0.060 (interquartile range, 0.030-0.107); mean, 0.063 (standard deviation, 0.054). All three gaps differed from zero. At least moderate loss occurred in 18 studies (36.7%) for training-to-internal testing, 27 studies (55.1%) for training-to-external testing, and 10 studies (20.4%) for internal-to-external testing. Precision-weighted pooled differences were 0.034 (95% confidence interval, 0.023-0.045), 0.061 (0.047-0.076), and 0.029 (0.018-0.040), respectively, closely matching unweighted results. Most reconstructed study-level gap confidence intervals included zero, including 36 of 49 (73.5%) training-to-external intervals. Despite the aggregate pattern of performance loss, 47 of 49 studies (95.9%) reached positive or cautiously positive conclusions. CONCLUSION: In this randomized, validation-enriched sample of recent PubMed-indexed radiomics studies, radiomics model discrimination declined across evaluation stages, with the largest loss between training and external testing. The aggregate pattern remained evident after precision weighting but was often inconclusive within individual studies. Although methodologically valuable, the presence of external validation alone did not establish preservation of performance relative to development.

articles.title: An accessible efficient intervertebral disc vision-language model training strategy with LLM-based retrieval method for spine MRI report generation.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Artificial intelligence (AI) has become increasingly important in healthcare, and multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities in understanding and integrating information from medical images and clinical text. This study explores a low-cost and effective MLLM-based approach for automated radiology report generation from lumbar spine MRI, aiming to improve reporting efficiency and consistency. METHODS: To mitigate the challenges of limited data availability and the high costs associated with applying MLLMs to spinal report generation, we proposed using the axial plane of a single lumbar intervertebral disc (IVD) and the adjacent vertebrae as the research subject. We constructed the pipeline of data processing to get disc-corresponding images and medical reports based on large language models (LLMs). Then, We fine-tuned presently mature MLLMs under conditions of 1125 patient samples and hardware limitations, achieving considerable results. RESULTS: In addition to performance evaluated using traditional natural language processing metrics, including BLEU (0.24), ROUGE-L (0.53), and CIDEr (1.28), we further validated the proposed strategy on clinical pathological classification tasks, achieving F1 scores of 0.93 for disc pathology, 0.81 for canal stenosis, and 0.91 for dehydrated disc. Notably, the model achieved diagnostic performance comparable to that of experienced radiologists for canal stenosis and dehydrated disc. These results demonstrate the feasibility of the proposed strategy. Furthermore, our experiments show that the LLM-based data evaluation pipeline is stable and reliable. CONCLUSION: This study offers a new perspective on the field of spinal reporting and outperforms existing methods on both performance and cost. Meanwhile, there is a considerable room for improvement in aspects of data volume and training scale.

articles.title: Virtual low-keV CT imaging enhances tumor contrast and provides favorable diagnostic assessability in oral cavity carcinoma: Comparison with MRI and polyenergetic CT.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Low-energy virtual monoenergetic imaging (VMI) improves tumor contrast in contrast-enhanced CT. Whether it can provide tumor delineation comparable to MRI in oral cavity carcinoma remains unclear. OBJECTIVE: To compare objective and subjective image quality, artifact burden, and two-dimensional tumor area measurements between 40-keV VMI, conventional polyenergetic CT images (PEI), and contrast-enhanced MRI in patients with oral cavity carcinoma. METHODS: Seventy-two patients (33 women; mean age, 70.2 ± 11.9 years) with newly diagnosed oral cavity carcinoma underwent contrast-enhanced MRI and dual-source dual-energy CT. Forty-keV VMI, PEI, and contrast-enhanced T1-weighted MRI with Dixon-based fat saturation were compared. Objective image quality was assessed using ROI-based measurements of tumor attenuation and contrast-to-noise ratio (CNR). Three readers independently noted 2D tumor dimensions and rated metal and motion artifacts as well as diagnostic assessability. RESULTS: Tumor attenuation was significantly higher in VMI than in PEI (median, 274.3 [IQR 236.7-316.5] vs 136.3 [114.9-154.5] HU), as was CNR (10.4 [6.6-15.8] vs 7.6 [3.3-11.9]; both p < 0.001). In five patients, severe metal artifacts rendered CT non-diagnostic. Among the 67 patients with evaluable examinations across all three modalities, median tumor area was 285.0 mm2 (IQR 195.0-705.0) in VMI, 320.0 mm2 (IQR 206.0-701.0) in PEI, and 312.0 mm2 (IQR 210.0-692.0) in MRI. The overall comparison was significant (p = 0.021), but no pairwise differences remained significant after correction for multiple comparisons. Metal artifacts were more pronounced in VMI than MRI (p < 0.001), whereas motion artifacts were more common in MRI (p < 0.001). Overall diagnostic assessability was higher for VMI and MRI than for PEI (both p ≤ 0.009). Inter-reader agreement was moderate to excellent (ICC ≥ 0.72). CONCLUSION: Low-energy VMI improves objective tumor attenuation and contrast-to-noise ratio compared with conventional PEI. Subjective diagnostic assessability ratings were favorable for both VMI and MRI, whereas metal artifacts were more pronounced in VMI and motion artifacts were more common in MRI. Although no pairwise differences in tumor area remained statistically significant after correction for multiple comparisons, these findings do not establish equivalence in tumor delineation or diagnostic performance compared with MRI.

articles.title: Modeling the carrying capacity and biology of pancreatic tumor organoids treated by chemotherapy and radiotherapy.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: Investigate the impact of treatments, including chemotherapy, radiotherapy, and chemoradiotherapy, on changing the carrying capacity of patient-derived tumor organoids (PDTOs). METHODS: We proposed novel mathematical modeling frameworks based on the logistic/Gompertz models and the growth dynamics of PDTOs post-treatment. We cultured PDTOs from different patients and treated them with 4 Gy radiation, chemotherapy (FOLFIRINOX at a previously determined organoid-specific IC50 dose), and combined regimens, respectively. At least 10 organoids per group were tracked and measured using brightfield images up to 14 days following each treatment to capture organoid growth dynamics data, which was used for model calibration. The accuracy and robustness of the modeling were comprehensively evaluated by the average normalized mean squared errors (NMSE), Akaike Information Criterion (AIC), and Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC). RESULTS: The logistic model with compression effects was selected as the optimal framework to describe organoid growth in the control group, enabling robust estimation of baseline carrying capacities. Under treatment, all modalities induced dynamic and patient-specific changes in carrying capacity. Chemotherapy exhibited dose-dependent and heterogeneous effects, ranging from transient stabilization and rebound at a low dose to rapid and sustained suppression at higher doses. Radiotherapy produced more consistent reductions across patients, albeit with distinct temporal profiles. Notably, combined chemoradiotherapy primarily led to rapid or substantial decreases in carrying capacity, stabilizing or enhancing the effects observed with single treatments, reducing inter-patient variability, and demonstrating a synergy effect that diminishes as drug levels increase. CONCLUSIONS: The results demonstrate that anticancer therapies modulate not only tumor size but also the underlying growth constraints (carrying capacities) in a dynamic and patient-specific manner. The proposed framework provides a novel perspective on tumor adaptation, resistance, regrowth, and a quantitative basis for understanding therapy-induced microenvironmental changes and long-term response; therefore, it holds promise for improving personalized treatment strategies and optimizing combination regimens.

articles.title: Magnetic resonance thermometry-based estimation of equivalent radiation dose and tumour control probability in combined radiotherapy and hyperthermia: a proof-of-concept and uncertainty study.
articles.abstract: To estimate the equivalent radiation dose in 2 Gy fractions (EQD2Gy) and tumour control probability (TCP) from probe based and magnetic resonance (MR) temperature measurements. In addition, we evaluate how uncertainties in MR thermometry affect these metrics in combined radiotherapy and hyperthermia for locally advanced cervical cancer (LACC).Approach: Temperature data were collected from three patients with LACC treated with radiotherapy and MR guided deep hyperthermia (MRgHT). Intraluminal vaginal probes provided temperature measurements at surrogate locations, while MR thermometry enabled voxel-wise temperature mapping within the target volume. These data were used to estimate EQD2Gy and TCP for combined radiotherapy and hyperthermia treatments. To assess the robustness of MR-based estimates, systematic and random temperature errors were introduced into MR thermometry data using Gaussian error models to simulate artefacts. The resulting impact on temperature distributions, EQD2Gy and TCP was evaluated using standard deviation analysis and dose volume histograms.Main results: Probe-based temperatures ranged from 39.1-39.7 °C, resulting in EQD2Gy and TCP enhancements of 2.4-4.3 Gy and 20-57 %, respectively. MR-based temperatures were higher (39.4-40.3 °C), yielding EQD2Gy (3.4-7.1 Gy) and TCP (22-68 %). Systematic temperature errors produced changes of up to 2 Gy in EQD2Gy and 5 % in TCP. In contrast, random errors - more representative of typical MR thermometry artefacts - led to minimal deviations, with changes of approximately 0.2 Gy in EQD2Gy. Within clinically relevant temperature ranges, overall uncertainties remained limited to 0.7 Gy for EQD2Gy and 1 % for TCP.Significance: MR thermometry enables voxel-based estimation of biological treatment enhancement in combined radiotherapy and hyperthermia. Despite inherent temperature uncertainties, MR-based EQD2Gy and TCP estimates remain robust within clinical accuracy limits, supporting their use for treatment evaluation and future hyperthermia-informed treatment planning.

articles.title: Capturing reader-specific annotation biases in ordinal classification: a controlled simulation study.
articles.abstract: Objective.Inter-reader variability remains a major challenge in medical image classification, particularly for tasks involving ordinal labels, due to subjective interpretation and institutional biases. While deep learning is widely used to automate and standardize such classification tasks, including breast density assessment, handling reader-dependent annotation behavior remains an open problem. This study introduces a controlled setting to assess the extent to which such variability can be captured by a reader-adaptive model.Approach.This work builds on ReaderAdaptNet, a recently proposed reader-adaptive framework that models individual annotation styles through jointly learned reader-specific embeddings. Through a simulation study, it aims to deepen the understanding of this framework and to address the evaluation limitations imposed by small expert-annotated datasets, for which the underlying bias mechanisms are neither known nor controllable. Synthetic reader profiles are generated to reproduce realistic annotation behaviors, enabling a controlled analysis of the model's ability to adapt to diverse annotation biases. The effects of the embedding dimension and of the fusion strategy of image-reader features on classification accuracy are assessed. The structure of the embedding space is also analyzed.Main results.Results show that reader embeddings effectively capture identifiable, systematic biases, with moderate embedding dimensionality being sufficient. Systematic threshold shifts are recovered, whereas stochastic variability is not learnable. Conditioning image-reader fusion through feature-wise linear modulation or cross-attention mechanisms enables the correction of view-related discrepancies. The learned embedding space further reveals meaningful clustering of annotation profiles, reflecting similarity in reader behavior.Significance.Overall, the proposed synthetic framework identifies which aspects of inter-reader variability are learnable by ReaderAdaptNet and provides a controlled proxy for anticipating model behavior in clinical settings.

articles.title: Advancing placenta accreta spectrum diagnosis: is 3-T MRI or combined MRI with ultrasound the answer?
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE: This study compares the diagnostic performance of US and 3-T MRIin diagnosing placenta accreta spectrum (PAS) disorder using final histopathological and surgical findings and explores the benefit of using a combined MRI and US approach to diagnose PAS. MATERIALS AND METHODS: We retrospectively reviewed electronic medical records of all patients undergoing 3-T MRIplacenta at our institution between January 2020 and November 2023. The gold standard for PAS outcome was histopathology, and where unavailable, we referred to the operative notes. Patients without surgical or histopathologic data, and non-diagnostic MRI studies were excluded. Sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV), negative predictive value (NPV), confidence intervals, and p-values were generated for MRI, US, and combined MRI + US to detect PAS with subgroup analysis for placenta accreta/increta and percreta. RESULTS: Eighty-eight patients met the inclusion criteria. The sensitivity and specificity of MRI for all PAS was 100.0% and 80.0% (p < 0.001), compared to US 89.5% and 62.0% (p < 0.001), and combined MRI + US 100.0% and 56.0% (p < 0.001), respectively. For diagnosing placenta percreta, MRI had a sensitivity and specificity of 83.3% and 94.3% (p < 0.001), compared to US 55.6% and 94.3% (p < 0.001) and combined MRI + US 83.3% and 92.9% (p < 0.001). CONCLUSION: Both US and 3-T MRIdemonstrated strong diagnostic performances for detecting PAS, with 3-T MRIdemonstrating stronger performance in this selective cohort, and not further improved by including US data. The continued use of US, MRI and clinical data for evaluating PAS disorder treatment options is recommended. KEY POINTS: Question No dedicated study has evaluated the diagnostic performance of 3-T MRIor the combined use of MRI with US in PAS. Findings 3-T MRIdemonstrates high sensitivity and specificity for diagnosing PAS. The combined MRI and US assessment does not further improve diagnostic performance for PAS. Critical relevance statement 3-T MRImay be particularly useful as an adjunct in selected high-risk patients, equivocal ultrasound cases, or cases requiring assessment of myoinvasive disease and multidisciplinary surgical planning.

articles.title: Classic signs in head and neck imaging-a quick guide for the radiology resident.
articles.abstract: Imagination has long played a critical role in scientific discovery. Historical figures such as Leonardo da Vinci combined careful observation with imaginative thinking to formulate ideas-such as early designs for flying machines-centuries before their eventual realisation. In radiology, a similar process underlies the recognition of imaging patterns and so-called "Aunt Minnies." Radiological signs serve as practical visual memory aids, facilitating the identification of pathology and supporting both education and day-to-day diagnostic workflow. This review covers a range of imaging signs in head and neck radiology, with a focus on their clinical relevance, practical implications, and potential interpretive pitfalls. Drawing on contributions from specialists in head and neck radiology, neuroradiology, and nuclear medicine, we illustrate both classic and less well-known signs, highlighting their diagnostic utility and limitations. KEY POINTS: Question Classic imaging signs aid diagnosis in head and neck radiology, but other pathologies can mimic their appearance, potentially leading to misinterpretation and diagnostic errors. Findings This review illustrates classic head and neck imaging signs across multiple modalities, highlighting their diagnostic relevance, principal mimics, and interpretive limitations. Critical relevance statement By critically examining the specificity and limitations of classic imaging signs, this review guides radiologists in integrating pattern recognition with differential diagnosis, helping avoid diagnostic pitfalls rather than relying on signs alone.

articles.title: Optical Spectroscopy and Machine Learning for Skin Cancer Detection: Why Cohort Size, Validation Rigor and Calibration - Not Architecture - Govern Clinical Readiness.
articles.abstract: Optical vibrational spectroscopy - principally Raman, with near-infrared (NIR) reflectance as a lower-cost proxy - combined with machine learning has been proposed as a non-invasive skin cancer triage adjunct, yet the field remains dominated by small single-centre cohorts and by deep networks reported without a matched classical baseline or leakage-free validation. The objective of this study is to determine whether architecture or methodology governs clinical readiness in this data regime. We synthesise 12 attributable optical skin cancer studies and benchmark seven models (four classical, three deep) under identical, fold-isolated preprocessing and patient-level grouped cross-validation on two public NIR cohorts, NIR-SC-UFES (647 spectra, 319 patients) and Deteccthia (152 lesion-level spectra), with discrimination, calibration, repeated and nested cross-validation, decision curve analysis and a three-class extension. Logistic regression reaches an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.774 (95% CI 0.709-0.838) versus 0.663 (0.596-0.727) for the best deep model (1D-CNN); classical models win in 20/20 seeds (Friedman p = 6.2 × 10⁻22) with lower seed-to-seed variance (Levene p = 0.0018). Deep models are significantly worse calibrated (Holm-adjusted p ≤ 0.024) and overfit within a median of 8-21 epochs. Platt scaling halves the expected calibration error (0.077 → 0.038). No model transported to the external cohort (all AUC ≤ 0.56; class signature correlation r =- 0.17). The ordering persists in the three-class task (macro AUC 0.829 versus 0.741). In this small-cohort regime, classical chemometric models match or exceed deep networks and calibrate more readily, and no single-instrument model survives external validation. Gains will come from larger multi-centre cohorts, patient-level leakage-free validation and probability calibration, not from deeper architectures.
